# Optimization {#optimization}

## Epigraph Form

In optimization, we often solve problems of the form

\begin{equation}
\min_{x} \quad J(x)
\end{equation}

where \(x\) is the decision variable and \(J(x)\) is the objective function.

The goal is to find the value of \(x\) that makes \(J(x)\) as small as possible.

The **epigraph form** rewrites this problem by introducing a new scalar variable \(z\). Instead of minimizing \(J(x)\) directly, we minimize \(z\), while forcing \(z\) to be an upper bound on \(J(x)\).

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
J(x) \leq z.
\end{equation}

So the original problem

\begin{equation}
\min_x J(x)
\end{equation}

is rewritten as

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
J(x) \leq z.
\end{equation}

The new variable \(z\) is not a penalty weight. It is not multiplied by the objective. It is simply an upper bound on the objective value.

---

<div style="background-color:#e8e6f5; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; margin-top:12px; margin-bottom:12px;">

## Example 1: Basic Epigraph Form

Consider the optimization problem

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad x^2.
\end{equation}

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
x^2 \leq z.
\end{equation}

This says: choose \(x\) and \(z\), make \(z\) as small as possible, but require that \(z\) stays above \(x^2\).

The optimal solution is still

\begin{equation}
x^\star = 0,
\qquad
z^\star = 0.
\end{equation}

So the epigraph form gives the same answer as the original problem.

</div>

---

## Why does this work?

The constraint

\begin{equation}
J(x) \leq z
\end{equation}

forces \(z\) to be at least as large as the objective value.

For any fixed \(x\), the smallest valid value of \(z\) is

\begin{equation}
z = J(x).
\end{equation}

So when we minimize \(z\), the optimizer will naturally push \(z\) down until it touches \(J(x)\).

At the optimum,

\begin{equation}
z^\star = J(x^\star).
\end{equation}

Therefore, minimizing \(z\) subject to \(J(x) \leq z\) is equivalent to minimizing \(J(x)\).

---

## Geometric meaning of the epigraph

The **epigraph** of a function \(J(x)\) is the set of all points lying on or above the graph of \(J(x)\).

Formally,

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{epi}(J)
=
\left\{
(x,z)
\;|\;
J(x) \leq z
\right\}.
\end{equation}

So the epigraph form means:

\begin{equation}
\text{Find the lowest point in the epigraph.}
\end{equation}

The variable \(z\) represents height. The constraint \(J(x)\leq z\) says that the point \((x,z)\) must lie above the function. Minimizing \(z\) pushes this point as low as possible.

---

<div style="background-color:#e8e6f5; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; margin-top:12px; margin-bottom:12px;">

## Example 2: Absolute Value Objective

Consider

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad |x|.
\end{equation}

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
|x| \leq z.
\end{equation}

The constraint

\begin{equation}
|x| \leq z
\end{equation}

is equivalent to

\begin{equation}
-z \leq x \leq z.
\end{equation}

So we can write

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
x \leq z,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
-x \leq z.
\end{equation}

This is useful because the nonsmooth objective \(|x|\) becomes a linear objective with linear constraints.

</div>

---

## Epigraph form for constrained optimization

Now consider a constrained optimization problem:

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad J(x)
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
h(x) \leq 0.
\end{equation}

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
h(x) \leq 0,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
J(x) \leq z.
\end{equation}

The original constraint \(h(x)\leq 0\) stays exactly the same.

The only thing we changed is the objective. Instead of minimizing \(J(x)\), we minimize \(z\), and we add the constraint \(J(x)\leq z\).

---

<div style="background-color:#e8e6f5; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; margin-top:12px; margin-bottom:12px;">

## Example 3: Constrained Epigraph Form

Consider

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad x^2
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
x \geq 1.
\end{equation}

We can write the constraint as

\begin{equation}
1-x \leq 0.
\end{equation}

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
1-x \leq 0,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
x^2 \leq z.
\end{equation}

The optimal solution is

\begin{equation}
x^\star = 1,
\qquad
z^\star = 1.
\end{equation}

Again, \(z^\star\) equals the optimal objective value.

</div>

---

## Turning constraints into a maximum condition

The epigraph form

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
h(x) \leq 0,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
J(x) \leq z
\end{equation}

can also be written using one maximum constraint.

Since both constraints must hold, we can combine them as

\begin{equation}
\max\{h(x), J(x)-z\} \leq 0.
\end{equation}

Why?

The condition

\begin{equation}
\max\{h(x), J(x)-z\} \leq 0
\end{equation}

means both terms inside the max must be less than or equal to zero:

\begin{equation}
h(x) \leq 0,
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
J(x)-z \leq 0.
\end{equation}

The second condition is equivalent to

\begin{equation}
J(x) \leq z.
\end{equation}

Therefore,

\begin{equation}
h(x)\leq 0,
\qquad
J(x)\leq z
\end{equation}

is equivalent to

\begin{equation}
\max\{h(x),J(x)-z\}\leq 0.
\end{equation}

---

## Inner and outer problem view

The epigraph form can also be viewed as an outer problem over \(z\) and an inner problem over \(x\).

Start from

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
\max\{h(x),J(x)-z\} \leq 0.
\end{equation}

For a fixed \(z\), define

\begin{equation}
\phi(z)
=
\min_x
\max\{h(x),J(x)-z\}.
\end{equation}

Then the epigraph problem becomes

\begin{equation}
\min_z \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
\phi(z) \leq 0.
\end{equation}

So we have two levels:

\begin{equation}
\text{Inner problem:}
\qquad
\phi(z)
=
\min_x
\max\{h(x),J(x)-z\}.
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\text{Outer problem:}
\qquad
\min_z z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
\phi(z)\leq 0.
\end{equation}

The inner problem asks:

\begin{equation}
\text{For this proposed upper bound } z,\text{ can I find an }x\text{ that satisfies everything?}
\end{equation}

The outer problem asks:

\begin{equation}
\text{What is the smallest upper bound }z\text{ that is feasible?}
\end{equation}

This is the form shown in the optimization block of your uploaded material. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}

<div style="background-color:#e8e6f5; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; margin-top:12px; margin-bottom:12px;">

## Example 4: Inner and Outer View

Consider

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad x^2
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
x \geq 1.
\end{equation}

Write

\begin{equation}
h(x)=1-x,
\qquad
J(x)=x^2.
\end{equation}

The epigraph max constraint is

\begin{equation}
\max\{1-x,x^2-z\}\leq 0.
\end{equation}

For a fixed \(z\), the inner problem is

\begin{equation}
\phi(z)
=
\min_x
\max\{1-x,x^2-z\}.
\end{equation}

If \(z<1\), then there is no feasible \(x\) satisfying both

\begin{equation}
x\geq 1
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
x^2\leq z.
\end{equation}

So \(z<1\) is impossible.

If \(z=1\), choosing \(x=1\) gives

\begin{equation}
1-x=0,
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
x^2-z=0.
\end{equation}

Therefore,

\begin{equation}
\max\{1-x,x^2-z\}=0.
\end{equation}

So \(z=1\) is feasible.

The outer problem chooses the smallest feasible \(z\), so

\begin{equation}
z^\star=1,
\qquad
x^\star=1.
\end{equation}

</div>

---

## Why \(z\) is added, not multiplied

A common confusion is why we write

\begin{equation}
J(x)-z
\end{equation}

inside the max instead of multiplying the objective by \(z\).

The reason is that \(z\) is an upper bound, not a weight.

The constraint

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z
\end{equation}

is equivalent to

\begin{equation}
J(x)-z\leq 0.
\end{equation}

That is why \(z\) appears by subtraction.

It is not trying to scale the objective. It is trying to represent the statement:

\begin{equation}
\text{objective value} \leq \text{upper bound}.
\end{equation}

So the correct expression is

\begin{equation}
J(x)-z.
\end{equation}

not

\begin{equation}
zJ(x).
\end{equation}

If we multiplied \(J(x)\) by \(z\), then \(z\) would become a weighting or scaling variable. That would be a different optimization problem.

---

## Feasibility interpretation

For each value of \(z\), the question is:

\begin{equation}
\text{Does there exist an }x\text{ such that }h(x)\leq 0\text{ and }J(x)\leq z?
\end{equation}

If yes, then \(z\) is feasible.

If no, then \(z\) is infeasible.

The optimal \(z^\star\) is the smallest feasible upper bound.

This gives an important interpretation:

\begin{equation}
z^\star
=
\text{best achievable objective value under the constraints}.
\end{equation}

---

## Monotonicity property

The feasible set in \(z\) is monotonic.

If a value \(z\) is feasible, then any larger value \(\bar{z}\geq z\) is also feasible.

Why?

If

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z
\end{equation}

and

\begin{equation}
\bar{z}\geq z,
\end{equation}

then automatically

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq \bar{z}.
\end{equation}

So making \(z\) larger relaxes the upper-bound constraint.

This means the outer problem often has a threshold structure:

\begin{equation}
z < z^\star
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\text{infeasible},
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
z \geq z^\star
\quad \Rightarrow \quad
\text{feasible}.
\end{equation}

This is why epigraph forms are often convenient for one-dimensional search over \(z\).

---

## Convexity property

Epigraph form is especially important in convex optimization.

A function \(J(x)\) is convex if and only if its epigraph is a convex set.

That means

\begin{equation}
J(x) \text{ is convex}
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
\mathrm{epi}(J)
=
\{(x,z):J(x)\leq z\}
\text{ is convex}.
\end{equation}

This is one of the most important properties of epigraphs.

It means that a convex objective can be converted into a linear objective with a convex constraint:

\begin{equation}
\min_x J(x)
\end{equation}

becomes

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

The objective \(z\) is linear, and the complexity is moved into the constraint.

---

<div style="background-color:#e8e6f5; padding:16px; border-radius:10px; margin-top:12px; margin-bottom:12px;">

## Example 5: Maximum Objective

Suppose we want to minimize the maximum of several functions:

\begin{equation}
\min_x \quad \max\{f_1(x),f_2(x),f_3(x)\}.
\end{equation}

Introduce \(z\) as an upper bound on all three functions.

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} \quad z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
f_1(x)\leq z,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
f_2(x)\leq z,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
f_3(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

This works because saying

\begin{equation}
\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x),f_3(x)\}\leq z
\end{equation}

is the same as saying every function is below \(z\).

This is useful because it replaces a max objective with multiple inequality constraints.

</div>

---

## Relation to minimax problems

Epigraph form is often used when the objective has a maximum:

\begin{equation}
\min_x \max_i f_i(x).
\end{equation}

The epigraph form is

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
f_i(x)\leq z,
\qquad
\forall i.
\end{equation}

So instead of minimizing the worst-case value directly, we minimize an upper bound on all possible values.

This is why epigraph form appears often in robust optimization, safety-constrained optimization, and multi-agent optimization.

---

## Relation to Lagrangian methods

For a constrained problem

\begin{equation}
\min_x J(x)
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
h(x)\leq 0,
\end{equation}

a Lagrangian method forms

\begin{equation}
L(x,\lambda)
=
J(x)+\lambda h(x),
\end{equation}

where \(\lambda\geq 0\) is a multiplier.

Here, the constraint is added as a penalty-like term.

By contrast, the epigraph form writes

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\end{equation}

subject to

\begin{equation}
h(x)\leq 0,
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

The key difference is:

\begin{equation}
\text{Lagrangian: constraint affects objective through a multiplier.}
\end{equation}

\begin{equation}
\text{Epigraph: objective becomes an upper-bound constraint.}
\end{equation}

The epigraph form does not multiply the objective or constraint by \(z\). It uses \(z\) as a target upper bound.

---

## Important properties

### Property 1: Same optimizer

The epigraph form has the same optimal \(x^\star\) as the original problem.

Original problem:

\begin{equation}
x^\star
=
\arg\min_x J(x).
\end{equation}

Epigraph form:

\begin{equation}
(x^\star,z^\star)
=
\arg\min_{x,z}
z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

At the optimum,

\begin{equation}
z^\star = J(x^\star).
\end{equation}

### Property 2: Converts objective into a constraint

The objective \(J(x)\) becomes the constraint

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

The new objective is simply

\begin{equation}
\min z.
\end{equation}

### Property 3: Useful for max objectives

A problem like

\begin{equation}
\min_x \max_i f_i(x)
\end{equation}

becomes

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
f_i(x)\leq z,
\quad
\forall i.
\end{equation}

### Property 4: Preserves convexity

If \(J(x)\) is convex and the constraints are convex, then the epigraph form is also convex.

### Property 5: Gives an upper-bound interpretation

The variable \(z\) always has the meaning

\begin{equation}
z = \text{candidate upper bound on the objective}.
\end{equation}

The optimizer searches for the smallest valid upper bound.

---

## Common mistake

A common mistake is to think that epigraph form changes the objective by weighting it.

That is not correct.

The epigraph form does not write

\begin{equation}
zJ(x).
\end{equation}

It writes

\begin{equation}
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

or equivalently,

\begin{equation}
J(x)-z\leq 0.
\end{equation}

So \(z\) is not a weight. It is an upper bound.

---

## Summary

The epigraph form rewrites

\begin{equation}
\min_x J(x)
\end{equation}

as

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

For constrained problems,

\begin{equation}
\min_x J(x)
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
h(x)\leq 0
\end{equation}

becomes

\begin{equation}
\min_{x,z} z
\quad
\text{s.t.}
\quad
h(x)\leq 0,
\quad
J(x)\leq z.
\end{equation}

The constraint \(J(x)\leq z\) says that \(z\) is an upper bound on the objective.

At the optimum,

\begin{equation}
z^\star = J(x^\star).
\end{equation}

So the epigraph form does not change the original problem. It rewrites it in a form that is often easier to analyze, easier to decompose, and useful for max objectives, constrained optimization, and convex optimization.
